ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

elbow imaging — clinical pattern 2

A child with a proximal ulnar injury has an elbow radiograph reviewed for associated damage. On adequate projections, the line along the radial neck fails to intersect the capitellum. The examiner confirms this is not simply an oblique projection. Which abnormality is suggested?

  1. Extension-type supracondylar humerus fracture
  2. Normal radiographic elbow alignment
  3. Olecranon fracture
  4. Radial head dislocation
  5. Traumatic elbow effusion with possible occult fracture
Answer and explanation

Radial head dislocation

A radiocapitellar line that fails to intersect the capitellum on adequate views raises concern for radial head malalignment.

Option explanations

Radial head dislocation: A radiocapitellar line that fails to intersect the capitellum on adequate views raises concern for radial head malalignment.

Traumatic elbow effusion with possible occult fracture: A visible posterior fat pad after trauma suggests an effusion and should prompt consideration of an occult intra-articular fracture. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Extension-type supracondylar humerus fracture: Posterior displacement of the distal humeral fragment can place the capitellum behind the anterior humeral line. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Normal radiographic elbow alignment: Normal radiocapitellar alignment and appropriate anterior humeral-line intersection support normal alignment but do not exclude every injury. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Olecranon fracture: A fracture through the posterior proximal ulna at the triceps insertion identifies an olecranon injury. This is not the pattern specified in this case.
